steps: Identify statutory criteria for issuing a building permit: §42 requires that filed building design documentation conforms to spatial plan/design specifications and requirements for construction works and building work.
Check registry evidence: authoritative records show plan_conformant=true, building_requirements_met=true, site_study_provided=true, competent_designer=true and fee_paid=true.

Check statutory grounds for refusal (§44): none of the refusal grounds (lack of competent author, missing site investigations, plan non-conformity, significant unmitigable environmental impact, national security danger, simultaneous incompatible permits, knowingly false information, etc.) are indicated in the authoritative records.
No additional prohibitions or special approvals (e.g., national security, environmental assessments) are recorded or asserted that would trigger refusal or NEED_MORE_INFO.
justification.text: Authoritative registry records show the application meets the statutory requirements (conformity to the detailed spatial plan and technical requirements, competent designer, site investigations performed and fee paid) and no refusal grounds under §44 are present, so the building permit should be granted.

steps: Verified payment of statutory fee per §40(2) (payment recorded).
Confirmed competent designer is documented (registry shows competent_designer=true), satisfying §42(1) and §40(2)/(3) requirements.

Checked substantive conformity: registry records plan_conformant=true, building_requirements_met=true, site_study_provided=true and plan_violation=false, indicating building design documentation conforms to spatial plan/design specifications and site investigations were provided as required by §42 and §14–§15.

Searched for registry evidence of any grounds for refusal under §44 (environmental impact, national security, ongoing repeal proceedings, building ban, simultaneous incompatible permits, knowingly false information); none are present in the authoritative records provided.
justification.text: Authoritative register entries show the statutory preconditions for issuing a building permit are met (fee paid, competent designer, design and site investigations conform to requirements) and no grounds for refusal under §44 are recorded; therefore the permit may be issued.

steps: Identify statutory conditions for issuing a building permit (§40–§42): building design documentation must conform to applicable spatial plan/design specifications and requirements for construction works; fee and required supporting documents must be provided; competent designer where required (§24, §40).

Check registry evidence: Dummy building registry (authoritative) shows plan_conformant=true, building_requirements_met=true, site_study_provided=true and plan_violation=false — indicating design documentation conforms and required site investigations are provided.

Check designer competence: Dummy designer competence registry (authoritative) shows competent_designer=true, satisfying the requirement that design documentation be created by a competent person or that qualifications are proven.
Check payment: Dummy state-fee payment ledger (authoritative) shows fee_paid=true, satisfying statutory payment requirement for processing (§29, §40(2)(8)).
Assess refusal grounds (§44): registry contains no indication of any manifest ground for refusal (plan_violation=false) and no other refusal grounds are shown in the records.

Conclusion based on authoritative records: all statutory preconditions recorded in the provided registers are satisfied and no refusal grounds appear, so the competent authority may issue the building permit.
justification.text: Authoritative registry entries show the application satisfies spatial-plan conformity, building requirements, site investigations, competent designer and fee payment, and no grounds for refusal are recorded; therefore the building permit can be issued under the Code.

steps: Identify statutory requirement: §24 and §44 require building design documentation for works subject to a building permit to be created by a competent person and §44(2) is a ground to refuse a permit if the documentation was not created by a competent person.

Check submitted factual record: Register entries (authoritative warrant) show plan_conformant=true, building_requirements_met=true, site_study_provided=true and competent_designer=true; state fee paid.
No record indicates an expert assessment is required under §14(3) nor any other formal deficiency in the application.

Although the applicant reports the designer is a relative and 'not a competent person', the designer registry is authoritative; absent verified evidence to the contrary the statutory competence requirement is satisfied.

Conclusion: on the available authoritative information, the statutory ground for refusal in §44(2) is not met, so the competent authority may issue the building permit. If the authority has reasonable doubts about competence it may require an expert assessment per §14(3).
justification.text: Authoritative register records confirm the building design documentation was created by a competent designer and all other formal requirements (plan conformity, site investigations, fee) are met; therefore the statutory ground for refusal (§44(2)) is not present and the building permit may be granted (subject to the authority-requested expert assessment if reasonable doubts arise).

steps: Identify statutory requirement: §42 requires that building design documentation conform to the detailed spatial plan or design specifications and to requirements for construction works in order for a building permit to be issued.
Identify statutory ground for refusal: §44(1) lists non-conformity with the spatial plan or design specifications as a ground for refusal to issue a building permit.

Assess evidence from registers: authoritative registry entries show plan_conformant = false and plan_violation = true (authoritative), while other procedural/technical conditions are satisfied (competent_designer = true, site_study_provided = true, fee_paid = true, building_requirements_met = true).
Apply law to facts: despite other requirements being met, the authoritative record of non-conformity with the spatial plan is a statutory ground for refusing the permit under §44(1).
justification.text: Authoritative registry data show the building design does not conform to the spatial plan (plan_violation), and §44(1) mandates refusal where the envisaged construction work does not conform to the spatial plan or design specifications, so the building permit must be refused.

steps: Identify legal rule: §42 requires building permit only where building design documentation conforms to requirements including the detailed spatial plan; §44(1) expressly requires refusal where the envisaged construction work does not conform to the detailed spatial plan.

Collect facts from inputs: applicant states municipality confirmed non-conformity (exceeds footprint and height); registry records (warrant=authoritative) indicate plan_conformant=true and plan_violation=false — a direct conflict on the key legal condition.

Assess reliability: registry entries are marked authoritative (not trust_only), but there is a contemporaneous statement that the local planning authority has confirmed non-conformity — the decision whether to issue a permit depends on which source correctly reflects the municipality's binding planning decision.
Under the statute the permit must be refused if the construction work does not conform to the detailed spatial plan; therefore determining conformity is dispositive for the outcome.

Because the available information about plan conformity is contradictory and the municipality's formal decision/record is not present or reconciled with the register, the factual prerequisite for applying §44 cannot be reliably determined.
justification.text: The statute mandates refusal if the work does not conform to the detailed spatial plan (§42, §44). The registry shows conformity but the local planning authority reportedly confirmed non-conformity; this decisive factual conflict must be resolved by a verified municipal decision or a corrected register entry before a permit decision can be made.

steps: Identify statutory preconditions for issuance per §42 and §40: building design documentation must conform to requirements and the application must include information regarding payment of the statutory fee and, where required, the energy performance certificate.

Examine authoritative registry records: Dummy building registry shows plan_conformant=true, building_requirements_met=true, site_study_provided=true and no plan_violation; designer registry shows competent_designer=true — these satisfy the core technical and competence grounds in §42 and §44 for issuing a permit.

Check payment evidence: the Dummy state-fee payment ledger is present but contains no payment particulars; §40(2)(8) requires information regarding payment of the statutory fee to be stated with the application.
Check energy performance certificate: statute (§40(2)(7) and §66) requires an EPC where applicable; the registers provided do not show an EPC or a statement whether one is required or filed.

Conclusion: essential technical and competence criteria are met in the authoritative records, but mandatory administrative information (proof of payment) is missing from the supplied records, and the presence or absence of a required energy performance certificate is not verifiable from the provided data.
justification.text: Authoritative records show conformity to plans, site studies and a competent designer, but the application must include proof of payment of the statutory fee and, where applicable, an energy performance certificate; those items are not present or verifiable in the supplied registers.

steps: Identify statutory documentary and procedural requirements for a building permit (incl. statement of payment of statutory fee) per §40(2) and §42.
Verify substantive prerequisites from registers: plan conformity, building requirements, site studies and competent designer are recorded as satisfied in authoritative registers.
Observe procedural gap: the state-fee payment ledger entry is marked unavailable in the submitted records, so statutory fee payment cannot be reliably verified.
Conclusion: substantive conditions appear met but procedural requirement (fee payment confirmation) is missing/unverifiable, so the decision cannot be made yet.
justification.text: The registries show the design and substantive requirements are satisfied and the designer is competent, but the statutory fee payment cannot be verified because the payment ledger is unavailable; confirmation/proof of fee payment is required before issuing the building permit.

steps: Identify statutory test: under §42 a building permit is issued if the filed building design documentation conforms to spatial plan/design specifications and requirements for construction works.
Authoritative register entries show plan_conformant=true, building_requirements_met=true and site_study_provided=true, which indicates the core technical conformity conditions are met.

Check refusal/mandatory-verification grounds in §44 and §40: a permit must be refused if the building design documentation was not created by a competent person or an expert assessment (where required) is missing; the application must also include proof of payment of statutory fee (§40(2)5).

Registry shows designer competence and fee payment only in a 'trust_only' record (self-report), i.e. unverified; there is no authoritative record of expert assessment (if one is required) or of environmental-impact/other approvals.

Because designer competence and fee payment are unverified and the record does not confirm whether any required expert assessment or required approvals/EIA have been completed, the statutory preconditions for issuing the permit are not fully verifiable from the supplied records.
justification.text: Authoritative data confirm plan conformity and technical requirements, but key application items (designer qualification, fee payment, any required expert assessment and approvals/EIA) are only self-reported or absent from the authoritative records, so the authority cannot lawfully issue the building permit until those items are verified.

steps: Identify controlling law: §119 allows a court to grant decision-making power in a significant matter to one parent.
Applicant asserts she was granted that power and can decide alone.
Verify facts in provided registers: population registry confirms applicant is a parent (authoritative).
Custody registry (authoritative) records sole_custody = false and delegated_decision_right = false, contradicting applicant's claim of a court-granted delegation.
Consent service shows both_parents_consent = false (no joint consent recorded).

Because an authoritative custody registry entry negates the claimed delegation and no court order or custody-record update is provided, the statutory prerequisite (court grant under §119) is not shown in the records.
justification.text: Authoritative custody records do not show a court delegation of decision rights and no court order was supplied; to decide under §119 we need the court ruling (or an authoritative registry entry) showing delegation and the specific matter covered.

steps: Records show both parents have joint legal custody and the applicant is a parent (registers authoritative).
No sole custody or prior delegation of decision-making to one parent is recorded (sole_custody=false, delegated_decision_right=false).
Both parents’ consent is not recorded and the other parent is unreachable, so delay in obtaining a joint declaration is likely.

Under §120(3) of the Family Law Act, if making a joint declaration would cause a delay conflicting with the child’s interests, one parent has the right to enter into necessary transactions and perform necessary acts in the interests of the child alone.
justification.text: Given joint custody and absence of sole custody or delegated decision rights, and because urgent medical decisions that would be harmed by delay fall under §120(3), the mother may act alone to consent to necessary treatment for the hospitalized child.

steps: Check parental status: population registry reports applicant_is_parent = true (authoritative).
Check custody: custody registry reports sole_custody = true (authoritative).
Statutory rule: §120(1)-(2) makes a parent with legal custody the child’s legal representative and §120(2)–(3) permits a parent with sole custody to represent the child alone.
Statutory right to information: §144 entitles a parent to request information about the child unless it conflicts with the child’s interests.
Conclusion: as parent with sole legal custody, the applicant may act alone to access the child’s data; absence of both-parents' consent (consent service) is not dispositive given sole custody.
justification.text: Registers (authoritative) show the applicant is the parent and holds sole legal custody; under §§120 and 144 a parent with sole custody is the child’s legal representative and may request information, so the applicant may act alone to access the child’s data. If the requested data or action falls into a category that by law requires court consent, separate consent may still be needed.

steps: Parents have joint legal custody and a joint right of representation (§116, §120).

A single parent may act without the other only in urgent/necessary cases to avoid delay harming the child’s interests (§120(3)) or for everyday matters when the child resides with that parent (§145(2)).
Registry records (authoritative) show no sole custody or delegated decision right and that both parents’ consent is absent.
The matter is not urgent, the mother is reachable and withholds consent, and no court has granted decision-making to the father.
justification.text: Under the Act a parent with joint legal custody may not unilaterally decide on non-urgent matters when the other parent is reachable and refuses consent; absent urgency, sole custody, or a court delegation, the father cannot decide alone (see §§120, 145).

steps: Check registers: population registry shows applicant_is_not_parent (authoritative); custody registry shows no sole_custody and no delegated_decision_right (authoritative); consent service shows both_parents_consent = false (authoritative).

Identify applicable law: §120 — only a parent who has legal custody is the child’s legal representative; guardians are legal representatives only after court appointment (§173–§179); third parties have no general right to represent a child.

Apply facts to law: applicant is not a parent, has not been recorded as having sole custody or delegated decision rights, and there is no recorded consent of both parents or record of a court-appointed guardian or other legal representative.
Conclude that, under the Family Law Act, the applicant is not authorised to decide on the child’s behalf or access the child’s data alone.
justification.text: Authoritative registers show the applicant is not a parent, has no sole custody or delegated decision rights, and both parents have not consented; the Act permits only a parent with legal custody or a court-appointed guardian to represent a child, so acting alone is not allowed.

steps: Identify legal rule: a parent who has legal custody is the child’s legal representative (§120).
Examine records: population registry (authoritative) indicates applicant_is_parent = true.
Examine custody records: custody registry (authoritative) shows no sole_custody and no delegated_decision_right, consistent with parental legal custody remaining with parent(s).
User’s self-report of being an aunt and lack of parental consent conflicts with authoritative registers; authoritative registers prevail for decision here under the given facts.
justification.text: Authoritative population and custody registers show the applicant is a parent and there is no sole custody or delegation; under §120 a parent with legal custody is the child’s legal representative, so representation is permitted despite the user’s claim to be an aunt.

steps: Registry: applicant_is_parent = true (authoritative) — applicant is the child's parent.
No custody entry indicating sole legal custody was found in the custody registry (fields empty).

Law: parents generally have joint legal custody (§§116, 117, 120) and must act jointly on significant matters; a parent with whom the child resides may decide everyday matters alone (§145(2)); §120 allows one parent to act alone if delay would conflict with the child's interests.
Consent service indicates both_parents_consent = false (i.e. other parent has not given blanket consent).

The case facts lack key items required to apply the statutory rules: whether the father has sole legal custody, whether the child resides with the father, whether the specific matter is an everyday/routine (non-essential) matter, and whether the mother gives consent for this act.

Because the matter is not urgent and the mother is reachable, the statutory pathway allowing unilateral action (everyday matters by the resident parent or acting to avoid delay harming the child) cannot be determined from available records.
justification.text: Registry proves you are a parent but contains no custody or residence information and consent is not recorded; to decide whether you may act alone under §§120 and 145 the court needs confirmation of custody status, where the child resides, whether the matter is an everyday (routine) matter, and whether the other parent consents.

steps: Registry: applicant_is_parent = true (authoritative) — applicant is a parent.
Registry: sole_custody = false and delegated_decision_right = false (authoritative) — no sole custody or delegated decision rights, i.e. parents have joint legal custody.
Statute §120(1),(2): parents with joint legal custody are the child’s legal representatives and have a joint right of representation.
Statute §120(7): if a parent represents a child independently, consent of the other parent is presumed; §144 gives parents rights to request information about the child.
Therefore as a parent with joint custody and legal representation, the applicant may access the child’s data without a recorded consent of the other parent.
justification.text: The registers show the applicant is a parent with joint legal custody; under §§120 and 144 a parent with legal custody is a legal representative entitled to act for and obtain information about the child, and consent of the other parent is presumed for independent representation.

steps: Default rule (§117) is that both parents have joint legal custody; representation is joint (§120).

A parent may represent the child alone for everyday (routine) matters if the child resides with that parent with the other parent's consent (§145(2)), or if powers of decision were granted by court (§119) or the parent has sole custody (§120(2)).
A parent may also act alone without consent in urgent cases where joint declaration would cause harmful delay (§120(3)), but the requester states there is no emergency and the father is reachable.

Registry data: population register confirms applicant is a parent; custody registry (which would show sole custody or delegated decision rights) is unavailable; consent service indicates both_parents_consent = false.
Because the custody registry is unavailable and there is no recorded consent, it cannot be confirmed under the statute that the mother may act alone for a non-urgent routine matter.
justification.text: The custody register (authoritative source for sole custody or delegated decision rights) is unavailable and there is no recorded consent from the other parent; absent an emergency, the law requires either sole/delegated custody or the other parent’s consent to act alone for routine matters.

steps: Identify applicable rule: §14 sets requirements—citizenship, at least secondary education, active legal capacity, Estonian proficiency; §14(2) allows EU citizens if they meet requirements; §14(2) also reserves certain sensitive posts to Estonian citizens only.
Check prohibitions in §15 (criminal convictions, family relationship with supervising official, other statutory preclusions).

Examine registry evidence: authoritative population registry indicates Estonian citizenship and full capacity; authoritative education registry confirms secondary education; authoritative language registry confirms Estonian proficiency; authoritative criminal registry shows no conviction.
Note discrepancy between applicant's self‑statement (Finnish/EU citizen) and authoritative population registry (shows Estonian citizen); authoritative registers outweigh unverified self-report.

No record or allegation of a statutory disqualification (criminal conviction) or family relationship with a supervising official appears in the authoritative records provided and the applicant has asserted no family conflict.
Conclusion: applicant satisfies statutory requirements to be employed in service for posts not reserved to Estonian citizens; outcome ALLOW.
justification.text: Authoritative registries confirm the person has (Estonian) citizenship or otherwise meets the §14 requirements (secondary education, full legal capacity, Estonian proficiency) and there is no criminal conviction or disqualifying family relationship recorded, so employment in service is permitted for posts not reserved to Estonian citizens.

steps: Identify statutory eligibility requirements in §14 (Estonian citizenship, at least secondary education, active legal capacity, Estonian proficiency).
Check registry records: ee_citizen=true, secondary_education=true, full_capacity=true, speaks_estonian=true, criminal_conviction=false.
Check disqualifications in §15 (criminal punishment, court deprivation, prohibited family relations) — registries show no conviction and applicant reports no supervising-family relationship.
Note procedural requirements (e.g. competition and appointing authority per §16 and §22) do not negate meeting substantive eligibility criteria.
Conclusion: on the provided facts and authoritative registry data, the applicant meets the statutory substantive requirements for employment in the civil service.
justification.text: The applicant satisfies the substantive requirements of §14 (citizenship, secondary education, legal capacity, Estonian proficiency) and has no disqualifying circumstances under §15 according to authoritative registries; therefore the statute permits employment (subject to the authority’s procedural recruitment/appointment steps).

steps: Identify statutory eligibility rule: §14(1) allows Estonian citizens with secondary education, active legal capacity and required Estonian proficiency to be employed in the service; §14(2) only extends this to EU citizens, not third-country nationals.

Check registries: authoritative population registry indicates ee_citizen = true and full_capacity = true; education registry shows secondary_education = true; language registry shows speaks_estonian = true; criminal-records registry shows criminal_conviction = false.
Check statutory disqualifications (§15): no conviction recorded; applicant asserts no family conflict with supervising official (no registry disqualification present).
Conclusion: all legal conditions for appointment under §14(1) are met according to authoritative registries and no statutory bar from §15 is indicated.
justification.text: Authoritative registries confirm the person is an Estonian citizen with secondary education, required Estonian proficiency, active legal capacity and no criminal conviction; under §14(1) such a person may be employed in the civil service, so the request is allowed.

steps: Identify statutory eligibility: §14 requires Estonian citizenship, at least secondary education, active legal capacity and Estonian proficiency; §15 disqualifies persons with certain criminal convictions or prohibited family relationships to a supervising official.
Check population registry (authoritative): ee_citizen = true, full_capacity = true → citizenship and legal capacity satisfied.
Check education registry (authoritative): secondary_education = true → education requirement satisfied.
Check language registry (authoritative): speaks_estonian = true → language requirement satisfied.
Check criminal-records registry (authoritative): criminal_conviction = false → no disqualifying criminal conviction recorded.
Applicant self-declared no family conflict with any supervising official; no authoritative family-relationship data was provided in the supplied registers.
justification.text: Authoritative registers show the applicant meets the §14 requirements (citizenship, education, capacity, Estonian proficiency) and no disqualifying convictions under §15; the applicant also self-declared no supervisory family conflict and no authoritative record contradicts that, so appointment is permitted on the supplied information.

steps: Identify statutory prerequisites for employment in service: Estonian citizenship, at least secondary education, active legal capacity and proficiency in Estonian (§14(1)).
Check population registry: ee_citizen = true and full_capacity = true (authoritative) — citizenship and legal capacity satisfied.
Check education registry: secondary_education = true (authoritative) — education requirement satisfied.

Check language registry: speaks_estonian = true (authoritative). Applicant self-reports lacking required Estonian, but authoritative registry entry indicates proficiency; authoritative data controls factual determination.
Check criminal-records registry: criminal_conviction = false (authoritative) — no disqualifying conviction under §15.
Applicant confirms no family conflict with supervising official (required confirmation under §15 clause on relatives).
All statutory preconditions for employment under §14(1) are met according to authoritative registry data and the applicant's declarations.
justification.text: Authoritative registry data and the applicant's declarations show Estonian citizenship, secondary education, active legal capacity, Estonian proficiency and no disqualifying conviction or family conflict, satisfying §14(1) and §15, so appointment is permitted.

steps: Verified applicant is Estonian citizen, has secondary education, active legal capacity and Estonian proficiency (§14) — supported by authoritative registries.
Checked registry for criminal record: authoritative criminal-records registry reports no criminal conviction.

Statutory disqualifications (§15) bar persons currently under punishment for an intentional crime or punished for certain state-related intentional offences; no registry evidence of such disqualification.
Applicant also declared no family conflict with supervising official, and no registry indicates kinship-related disqualification (§15(4)).
Applicant's self-report of a past conviction conflicts with authoritative registry; registry data are authoritative and take precedence for decision.
justification.text: Under §14 the applicant meets the formal requirements and the authoritative criminal-records registry shows no disqualifying conviction or ongoing punishment under §15, so employment in civil service is permitted.

steps: Confirm applicant is a consumer and the contract was concluded at a distance (registry: is_consumer=true, distance_contract=true, authoritative).
Confirm the goods are not in an excluded category under § 53(4) (registry: excluded_category=false, authoritative).

Check withdrawal time limit: statutory right to withdraw within 14 days from entry into a distance contract (§ 56(1)); contract was concluded 5 days ago and withdrawal notice was sent yesterday, so it was sent within the 14-day period.
Conclude that statutory requirements for exercising the right of withdrawal are met (no excluded category, consumer, distance contract, notice timely).
justification.text: Under § 56(1) a consumer may withdraw from a distance contract within 14 days; the records confirm you are a consumer, the sale was a distance contract and the laptop is not excluded, and your withdrawal notice was sent within the 14‑day period, so withdrawal is permitted.

steps: Identify statutory eligibility requirements (§14): Estonian citizenship (or EU citizen under law), at least secondary education, active legal capacity, and proficiency in Estonian.

Check registers: education_registry shows secondary_education=true; population_registry shows full_capacity=true and eu_citizen=false; language_registry shows speaks_estonian=true; criminal_records_registry shows criminal_conviction=false.

Determine missing/uncertain facts: registers do not state whether the applicant is an Estonian citizen (eu_citizen=false only rules out EU citizenship); the statutory prohibition on employing persons with certain family relations to supervising officials (§15 clause 4) requires verification that no such relationship exists — the applicant's self-confirmation is not independently verified in the provided records.

Conclude that, because citizenship status and independent verification of prohibited family relationship are absent or unverified, the statutory eligibility cannot be decided on the given information.
justification.text: Secondary education, legal capacity, Estonian proficiency and absence of convictions are present in the records, but the applicant's Estonian citizenship (or lawful EU status) is not shown and the absence of a prohibited family relationship to a supervising official is only a self-declaration and not independently verified; these missing items are necessary to determine eligibility under §§14 and 15.

steps: Check statutory eligibility: §14 requires Estonian citizenship, at least secondary education, active legal capacity and Estonian proficiency — verify registries.
Verify disqualifying grounds in §15 (criminal punishments, court bans, and prohibited family relations with supervising official).

Registry data available and authoritative show: ee_citizen true, secondary_education true, full_capacity true, speaks_estonian true, criminal_conviction false — these meet §14 and not disqualifying under §15 clauses 1–3.

§15 clause 4 (prohibited family relations with a supervising official) must be assessed: applicant self-confirms absence of such relation, but no authoritative registry evidence of family ties is available because the population registry entry is marked unavailable.
Because prohibition based on family relations is a categorical statutory bar, authoritative verification (population registry or equivalent) or other reliable evidence is required before appointment.
justification.text: Citizenship, education, capacity, language and criminal-history checks in the provided registries satisfy §14–§15 except for the nepotism prohibition in §15(4); authoritative verification of family ties to any supervising official (population registry or equivalent) is missing and necessary to decide.

steps: Identify statutory prerequisites for employment (§14): Estonian citizenship (for certain posts), at least secondary education, active legal capacity, proficiency in Estonian.
Check registries: education and Estonian language proficiency are present with authoritative warrants; criminal record is authoritative and clear (no conviction).
Population/citizenship and full legal capacity appear only in a register entry with warrant 'trust_only' (unverified self-report).
Applicant has self-confirmed absence of family conflict, but there is no authoritative record verifying absence of disqualifying familial relationships under §15(4).

Because Estonian citizenship, active legal capacity and absence of disqualifying family ties are either unverified or based only on self-report, the statutory requirement of verified eligibility cannot be confirmed.
justification.text: Secondary education, language proficiency and clean criminal record are confirmed authoritatively, but Estonian citizenship, active legal capacity and absence of disqualifying family ties are only self-reported (trust_only) and must be verified before appointment under §§14 and 15.

steps: Registry shows buyer is a consumer and the sale is a distance contract (authoritative).
Product is not in an excluded category per registry (authoritative).
User states purchase was 5 days ago and withdrawal notice was sent yesterday, which is within the 14‑day withdrawal period under §56(1) and §56(2¹).
No indication this is a financial service or other exception that would remove the right of withdrawal.
justification.text: Given the authoritative records that this was a distance sale of a non‑excluded product and the consumer sent the withdrawal within the 14‑day period, the statute entitles the consumer to withdraw, so the request is allowed.

steps: Registry confirms the purchase is a distance contract with a private consumer (is_consumer=true, distance_contract=true).
The goods were received 5 days ago and the consumer sent the withdrawal notice today, which is within the 14-day withdrawal period under §56(1)–(1¹).

Product catalogue record shows excluded_category=false, so the headphones are not in an exception list (e.g. personalised goods, perishable goods, sealed hygiene items, unsealed audio/video recordings) under §53(4).
No registry data indicates the contract is for financial services, digital content, or that the consumer validly waived the right of withdrawal under the statutory exceptions.
Therefore the statutory right of withdrawal applies and the consumer may withdraw.
justification.text: Under §56 a consumer may withdraw from a distance contract within 14 days; the registers confirm a distance sale and that the headphones are not in an excluded category, so withdrawal is permitted.

steps: The Law of Obligations grants a 14‑day right of withdrawal to a consumer for distance contracts (§56(1)).
The Subchapter applies only to contracts between a trader and a consumer, so withdrawal right exists only if the buyer is a consumer.
Authoritative registry record marks is_consumer = true and distance_contract = true, indicating the purchase is covered by the consumer distance-contract rules.
Product catalogue record shows excluded_category = false, so no statutory exception (e.g., custom or perishable goods) bars withdrawal.
The requester states the 14‑day period is still running and that a withdrawal notice was sent yesterday, so timing requirement appears satisfied.
justification.text: Authoritative registry data classify the purchase as a consumer distance contract and the product is not in an exclusion category; given the withdrawal notice was sent within the 14‑day period, the statutory right of withdrawal applies and the withdrawal is allowed.

steps: The purchase is a distance contract by authoritative registry (distance_contract = true) and the product is not in an excluded category (excluded_category = false).
Under §56(1) the consumer has a 14-day withdrawal period which here expired six weeks after delivery.

§56(1⁶) extends the withdrawal period up to 12 months if the trader violated the obligation to provide the information about the right of withdrawal required by clause 12 of §54(1); if the trader belatedly provided that information within 12 months the consumer then has 14 days from receipt.
The available records do not state whether or when the trader provided the clause-12 precontractual information or whether the trader provided the confirmation required by §55 on a durable medium.
Whether the late withdrawal is valid depends on those missing facts (compliance with clause 12 and date of receipt).
justification.text: The 14-day statutory withdrawal period has expired, but the consumer may still withdraw if the trader failed to provide the clause-12 precontractual information (or provided it only later); the registers do not show whether or when that information or the §55 confirmation was given, so more information is required.

steps: Identify statutory rule: §56 grants 14-day withdrawal right for distance contracts unless an exception in §53(4) applies (e.g., goods made to consumer specifications).
Check authoritative registers: trader CRM confirms this is a distance contract with a consumer (is_consumer=true, distance_contract=true).
Check product catalogue (authoritative): excluded_category=false, i.e. catalogue does not mark the item as falling into §53(4) exclusions (not flagged as made-to-order).
Applicant states the withdrawal was sent yesterday and the 14-day period has not expired (no register contradicting this).
Conclusion: statutory exclusion for custom-made goods does not appear to apply per authoritative catalogue record, and the consumer submitted a timely withdrawal, so withdrawal is permitted.
justification.text: Authoritative registry data show a distance contract with a consumer and that the product catalogue does not classify the item as an excluded made-to-order category; the applicant reports a timely withdrawal within the 14-day period, so under §56 the withdrawal is effective and permitted.

steps: Confirm contract is a distance contract: registry indicates distance_contract = true (authoritative).
Check whether the contract type is excluded from the right of withdrawal: product_catalogue shows excluded_category = false (authoritative).
